title: My Daily Brief
overview: A first-ever three-way summit of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders in Shenzhen produced a joint 'peace declaration' but no binding agreements, while fighting over the Crimean Bridge intensified. Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq in the largest IPO on record, the UN's top court found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, and Elon Musk distanced himself from MAGA after heavy Republican midterm losses. Also covered: a South Korean ruling on former PM Han Duck-soo, a Chase vendor data breach, a North Carolina utilities commissioner's resignation, and Susan Smith's parole denial.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first three-way meeting, discussing nuclear arms and Ukraine
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin met for more than an hour on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first meeting of its kind. Trump called it historic and said the three countries are 'uniquely positioned' to discuss reducing nuclear weapons. Xi called for nuclear weapons to be prohibited and destroyed, and Putin spoke of shared responsibility for peace. No arms control agreement or Ukraine breakthrough was announced. Trump also held separate meetings with Xi and Putin, and later criticised the International Criminal Court as 'out of control.'
key_facts: It was the first trilateral meeting of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders; it lasted more than an hour.
The New START treaty, the last US-Russia nuclear arms pact, expired in February; Trump wants a new deal that includes China.
China has more than 600 warheads, compared with more than 5,000 believed to be held by each of the US and Russia.
Trump and Putin met separately for about 40 minutes, their first talks since the Alaska summit in 2025.
Trump said: 'We are really making history.'

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS (AP) stressed that there was no breakthrough and that Putin gained global stature. They highlighted European and Ukrainian suspicion, Merz's fear of another 'Anchorage moment', Yalta comparisons, and Trump's ICC criticism given Putin's arrest warrant. The Guardian described both Trump and Putin as fighting 'failing wars of choice.'

The Korea Herald (AP) and The Hill presented it as a possible historic pivot or a forgettable photo op. They quoted experts such as Daryl Kimball who kept expectations low, and covered the Iran, trade and Taiwan side discussions.

The New York Post focused on the optics, arguing that Putin was snubbed and diminished by Chinese protocol while Trump got a warm welcome. It quoted analysts who said this reflected Beijing courting Trump. The Daily Caller emphasised the historic nature of the meeting and Trump's argument for engaging with rivals.

disputed: Whether the summit will lead to sustained arms control talks or was mainly symbolic.
Whether Putin's protocol treatment in China signals anything about Beijing's stance; a Eurasia Group analyst cautioned against reading too much into it.
Putin said Russia accepted a US-proposed compromise from Anchorage and that Ukraine should accept it; Ukraine and Europe previously rejected those proposals.
stories.why: The three largest nuclear powers met at a time when there is no arms control treaty in force and wars are ongoing in Ukraine and Iran.

stories.headline: US, China and Russia issue joint 'peace declaration' after Shenzhen summit
stories.summary: After their summit, the three leaders issued a four-point declaration. It covered UN reform, increased production of refined petroleum products, criticism of the International Criminal Court and similar bodies for 'abusing their jurisdiction', and a pledge to discuss nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation. It restated that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought' but set no binding limits or timelines. Xi called the meeting 'fruitful', and Putin rejected the view that it was a photo op. Trump plans a White House press conference on Friday.
key_facts: The declaration has four points: UN reform, refined petroleum supply, ICC jurisdiction and nuclear risk dialogue.
The nuclear war language matches earlier statements by the five permanent UN Security Council members.
The declaration contains no binding arms reductions, deadlines or plan to end the wars in Ukraine or Iran.
Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant issued in March 2023.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian stressed that the declaration made no mention of the Ukraine and Iran wars. It quoted analysts who called the summit mostly symbolic and a win for Putin and for Beijing's agenda-setting. Al Jazeera briefly highlighted Xi's call for joint efforts on peace.
The Korea Herald (AFP) and The Hill reported the text factually, noting that it was first published by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, and quoted Xi's upbeat remarks.

Fox News presented it as a historic declaration and quoted extensively from the White House and Chinese statements. The Daily Caller called it historic but detailed its limits, including the absence of binding cuts, the hurdles to UN reform and China's arsenal growth.

disputed: Accounts differ on the White House release: AFP said nothing had come from the White House at first, while Fox and the Daily Caller cite a White House statement.
Reported meeting length varies, from 'more than an hour' to about 1 hour 20 minutes.
It is unclear when nuclear talks would start or whether they would aim for binding limits.
stories.why: The statement shows where the three powers agree, including on curbing the ICC, and leaves the most pressing conflicts unaddressed.

stories.headline: Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq in largest IPO on record
stories.summary: Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, began trading under the ticker ANT. Shares opened at $111.50, well above the $83 IPO price that valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. The company sold 980 million shares, raising about $81 billion, which surpasses SpaceX's June IPO. Filings show fast revenue growth alongside large accounting losses, about $900 billion in computing commitments, and warnings about catastrophic AI risks. Supporters see the listing as easing AI funding worries, while others point to bubble fears and possible regulation from an incoming Democratic-led Congress.
key_facts: The IPO was priced at $83 a share, above the initial range of $70 to $78; 980 million shares were offered.
Shares opened at $111.50; CNBC reported they traded around $96 by early afternoon.
The company has about $900 billion in spending commitments, roughly $70 billion of it due within 12 months.
Anthropic carries $6.2 billion in debt and is unprofitable under standard accounting rules.
Founders keep 50.1% of voting power, and a Long-Term Benefit Trust generally selects a majority of the board.

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) emphasised investor bubble fears, public anxiety about AI, debt and spending strain, and the regulatory threat. The Verge highlighted CEO Dario Amodei's safety pledges and the risks disclosed in the filing, such as 'self-preserving' AI and agents escaping test environments.
CNBC framed the IPO as a boon to AI-linked stocks and a 'clearing event' for funding concerns. DW cast it as a test of investor appetite amid bubble worries. The Hill gave the basic figures.
Fox Business focused on strong demand and deal mechanics, including lock-ups, the retail allocation and revenue growth. It also noted the 'end of humanity' risk disclosure.

disputed: Valuation at the open differs: DW put it at $2 trillion, while others cite the $1.5 trillion IPO valuation.
Total funds raised differ by source: about $81 billion from the IPO, $26 billion from a private placement, and CNBC's figure of more than $100 billion overall.
Reported losses cover different periods: an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half versus $104 billion over nine months, both mostly from noncash charges.
The Hill dated the opening to Wednesday; other outlets say Thursday.
stories.why: The listing is a major test of whether public markets will fund the enormous costs of building AI.

stories.headline: Musk says he is 'not MAGA' and regrets midterm spending; Trump responds
stories.summary: Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said he is 'not MAGA.' He also said he felt 'pretty foolish' about spending record sums backing Republicans who lost badly in the midterms, though he added that results might have been worse without it. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, along with Texas's Senate race and governorship. Trump called Musk 'a friend' but said that when people veer from MAGA 'they don't do very well.' Democrats have promised scrutiny of tech firms, and one senator told Musk he is 'still getting a subpoena.'
key_facts: Musk was the top individual donor of the midterms, with figures cited ranging from about $442 million to $474 million.
Democrat James Talarico beat Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, and Gina Hinojosa defeated Gov. Greg Abbott.
Musk said: 'If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.'
Sen. Ruben Gallego responded: 'You are still getting a subpoena.'

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) framed the remarks as tech titans scrambling to rebrand after aligning with Trump for contracts and favourable policy. It drew a parallel with Palantir CEO Alex Karp's claim to be progressive.

BBC detailed the size of Musk's spending, his ties to government, and possible consequences for his businesses, such as data centre limits and probes into SpaceX contracts. Axios and The Hill emphasised that the Trump-Musk relationship has survived repeated breaks.
The New York Post and Washington Examiner led with Trump's 'warning' to Musk and contrasted Musk's earlier 'dark MAGA' persona. The Post included Gallego's subpoena retort.

disputed: Musk's spending for Paxton varies by source: at least $45 million (BBC), more than $150 million (NY Post) and around $200 million (PBS).
Accounts differ on when Trump spoke to NBC: Tuesday per the NY Post, Thursday per others.
It is unclear whether Musk faces congressional investigation.
stories.why: The richest political donor is publicly reassessing his alliance just as Democrats prepare to oversee tech companies.

stories.headline: South Korea's Supreme Court sends ex-PM Han Duck-soo's insurrection case back for retrial
stories.summary: South Korea's Supreme Court, sitting as a full bench, overturned part of the appeals ruling that sentenced former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo to 15 years for his role in Yoon Suk Yeol's December 2024 martial law. It found insufficient evidence that Han intended to subvert the constitution when he proposed a Cabinet meeting before the declaration. It upheld findings on his conduct after the declaration, as well as convictions for document falsification and perjury. The Seoul High Court will retry the case, and Han stays in custody for two more months. Separately, the court upheld a four-year sentence for Yoon's wife, Kim Keon Hee.
key_facts: Han, 77, was first sentenced to 23 years in January; the sentence was cut to 15 years on appeal in May.
Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae said the martial law declaration was unquestionably unconstitutional and illegal.
Yoon was sentenced to life in February, and his appeal ruling is scheduled for Jan. 26.
The special prosecutors said they respect the ruling.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera reported the retrial order factually. It noted Han's denial of all charges except perjury and gave background on Yoon's ouster.

Yonhap, the Korea Herald, CNA and DW reported the legal detail of which findings were upheld and which were overturned. They stressed the court's affirmation that the martial law was illegal and noted the Kim Keon Hee ruling.

disputed: The sentence Han will receive on retrial is unknown.
Han denies wrongdoing on all charges except perjury.
stories.why: The ruling shapes how South Korea holds senior officials accountable for the 2024 martial law crisis.

stories.headline: UN's top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled 9-6 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in its 2017 military campaign in Rakhine state. It is the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judges rejected Myanmar's argument that it was conducting counterinsurgency operations. The court ordered reparations, the safe return of refugees, and the prosecution of perpetrators, though it has no enforcement power beyond referral to the UN Security Council. The case was brought by Gambia, and observers say it may influence South Africa's genocide case against Israel.
key_facts: The vote was 9-6, read out by ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa.
The court estimated about 10,000 Rohingya were killed and all or parts of 392 villages were burned.
More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh; more than a million now live in camps there.
Britain said it is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché and called for a Security Council session.
Myanmar had not responded at the time of reporting.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian, PBS (AP) and NPR centred survivors' voices and the celebrations in the camps. They emphasised the precedent for the Gaza case and the limits on enforcing the ruling.
DW, Axios and The Hill focused on the court's legal findings and remedies and Rohingya activists' reactions. Axios also flagged the implications for the Israel case.

disputed: It is unclear whether Myanmar will comply, since the court cannot enforce its rulings.
The number who fled is reported as about 700,000 to more than 740,000.
How the ruling will affect the Gaza case is speculative.
stories.why: It is a first-ever state genocide ruling and may set the legal bar for future cases.

stories.headline: Chase says hackers may have accessed customer names and emails through vendors
stories.summary: JPMorgan Chase said third-party vendors were hit by a cyberattack in which attackers may have accessed marketing data, including some customer names and email addresses. The bank said its services were not disrupted, and it will contact affected customers and offer free credit monitoring. Chase said the breach is unrelated to a software bug that delayed payments across several banks and Zelle earlier in the week. The incident comes amid a string of US outages that officials say were not caused by cyberattacks.
key_facts: The data accessed may include customer names and email addresses held by vendors.
Chase did not name the vendors or say how many customers were affected.
Monday's banking disruption was blamed on a software bug in Chase's on-premises hardware.
Officials told a House committee they had found no evidence of cyberattacks behind recent outages, including an FAA ground stop.

perspectives.framing: WBTV and The Hill reported Chase's statement plainly and stressed that the breach is unconnected to the earlier outage.

The Daily Caller and Washington Examiner placed the breach within a broader pattern of outages, such as the FAA, the NSA network and Microsoft. They noted lawmakers' national security concerns and the separate Optimizely web-skimming attack.

disputed: The vendors involved and the number of affected customers are unknown.
Any link to the Optimizely incident is unconfirmed; Chase did not mention it.
Some lawmakers fear the recent outages are connected despite officials' denials.
stories.why: Chase customers may be targeted with phishing using the exposed contact details.

stories.headline: NC utilities commissioner resigns days after Duke Energy rate increase approved
stories.summary: North Carolina Utilities Commissioner Donald van der Vaart will resign effective Jan. 1, 2027, State Treasurer Brad Briner announced. The announcement came two days after the commission approved Duke Energy rate increases. No reason for the resignation was given. WFAE reported that van der Vaart had been a frequent dissenter and, after repeated absences, was left out of the Duke rate case and Carbon Plan proceedings. Gov. Josh Stein called the rate increase 'too high', and Briner will appoint a replacement.
key_facts: The commission approved the Duke rate hikes on Nov. 16; Queen City News reports a 9.5% increase over two years.
Some customers could see nearly $10 more a month starting in January.
Van der Vaart served about a year and a half on the five-member commission.

perspectives.framing: WFAE focused on van der Vaart's record as a dissenter, including his support for coal and data centre rules and opposition to solar, and on his absences from major cases.
WBTV linked the resignation's timing to the rate decision without stating a cause, and included Stein's criticism. The other local outlets focused on bill impacts.

disputed: The reason for the resignation has not been disclosed.
stories.why: Duke customers face higher bills, and the treasurer will pick a new regulator.

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge a third time this week; Putin vows 'far more painful' response
stories.summary: Ukraine hit the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge for the third time this week on Thursday, using Neptune missiles by its own account. The strike briefly halted rail traffic. A strike on Tuesday had collapsed part of the road section, which is closed for the foreseeable future. Speaking after the Shenzhen summit, Putin promised a response 'far more painful' than Kyiv's attack and said talks on halting sea and energy strikes were now off. Zelensky was in Berlin for talks with more than 40 partners, along with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
key_facts: Russia's transport ministry said no one was hurt in Thursday's strike, and rail service resumed that afternoon.
About 200 metres of roadway fell into the sea after Tuesday's strike.
Putin said: 'After the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, there will be no agreements.'

perspectives.framing: BBC and DW detailed the damage and the bridge's military and symbolic role, and noted Russian strikes on Kyiv's bridges. A Hill opinion piece argued that Zelensky is no longer seeking Trump's permission.
Fox News led with Putin's threat and paired it with US-European peace efforts in Berlin, quoting Kushner that Trump is determined to end the war.

disputed: Putin says the bridge is purely civilian, while Kyiv calls it a main military crossing.
Repair estimates vary, from a few months for some sections (according to TASS) to an indefinite closure for road traffic.
stories.why: The strikes and Putin's threat could escalate the war just as peace talks are underway.

stories.headline: Susan Smith denied parole for second time, 32 years after drowning her sons
stories.summary: South Carolina's parole board unanimously denied parole to Susan Smith, 55, who drowned her sons Michael, 3, and Alex, 14 months, in 1994. Smith expressed remorse at the hearing, said she is 'not the same person', and disputed prosecutors' account of her motive. The boys' father, David Smith, and the original prosecutors opposed her release, with David Smith calling the killings deliberate. She can apply again in 2028.
key_facts: The seven-member board's vote was unanimous; release would have required two-thirds of members present.
Smith initially claimed a Black man had carjacked her before she confessed nine days later.
This was her second parole denial, after the first in November 2024.

perspectives.framing: BBC and the Charlotte stations quoted both Smith's apology and David Smith's opposition at length. They recounted the false carjacking claim and her defence's mental-health argument.

disputed: Her motive remains disputed: prosecutors cite an affair, which Smith denies, attributing the crime to her mental health.
stories.why: The decision keeps one of the country's most notorious child-murder cases in the public eye.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: No articles directly addressed US or EU AI regulation. In passing, AP coverage of Anthropic's IPO mentioned a potential regulatory crackdown by the incoming Democratic-led Congress, and Musk coverage noted Democrats' pledges to scrutinise tech firms and data centres.
